title: ASIC Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution
legislative_instrument: RG 271 (issued 2 September 2021); enforceable paragraphs given legal effect by ASIC Corporations, Credit and Superannuation (Internal Dispute Resolution) Instrument 2020/98
licence: ASIC regulatory guide (copyright ASIC). Paraphrased only; consult the published guide.
verification_notes: Checked against the published PDF (rg271-published-2-september-2021.pdf) downloaded from asic.gov.au on 2026-10-19; the ASIC page lists no later reissue. Paragraph numbers and timeframes confirmed directly from the PDF text, including Table 2 (maximum IDR timeframes) and the 'Enforceable paragraph' markers. Enforceable paragraphs are binding on AFS licensees because s912A(1)(g)(i) requires IDR procedures to comply with ASIC standards and requirements, which ASIC Instrument 2020/98 sets by reference to those paragraphs (per RG 78 Appendix 1); the instrument itself was not opened. Non-enforceable paragraphs (for example RG 271.51 on acknowledgement) are ASIC expectations. AS/NZS 10002:2014 referenced in the guide has been reissued as AS 10002:2022, but RG 271 still refers to the 2014 definition. Private health insurers are not AFS licensees for health insurance products (Corporations Act s765A(1)(c)), so RG 271 does not govern PHI health insurance complaints, which are handled under the Private Health Insurance framework and the Commonwealth Ombudsman (Private Health Insurance Ombudsman); a PHI insurer's general or life insurance distribution under an AFS licence would be covered.
superseded_standards: RG 165 Licensing: Internal and external dispute resolution (for complaints received before 5 October 2021; withdrawn 5 October 2022)
companion_guidance: ASIC Regulatory Guide 267 Oversight of the Australian Financial Complaints Authority
ASIC Corporations, Credit and Superannuation (Internal Dispute Resolution) Instrument 2020/98
ASIC Corporations (Internal Dispute Resolution Data Reporting) Instrument 2022/205
AS/NZS 10002:2014 Guidelines for complaint management in organizations (reissued as AS 10002:2022)
General Insurance Code of Practice; Life Insurance Code of Practice
summary: RG 271 sets ASIC's standards and requirements for internal dispute resolution by financial firms, applying to complaints received on or after 5 October 2021. It adopts the AS/NZS 10002:2014 definition of complaint (including qualifying posts on the firm's own social media), sets maximum IDR response timeframes (30 calendar days for standard complaints, with special timeframes for superannuation, traditional trustee and certain credit complaints), prescribes the content of IDR responses and delay notifications (including the right to go to AFCA and AFCA's contact details), requires written responses for declined insurance claims and claim value disputes even when closed within 5 business days, and imposes board accountability and processes for identifying systemic issues. Enforceable paragraphs are binding via ASIC Instrument 2020/98.

clauses.heading: Application date
clauses.text: The standards, requirements and guidance in RG 271 apply to complaints received on or after 5 October 2021. Earlier complaints remained under RG 165, which was withdrawn on 5 October 2022.
clauses.notes: All current complaints are subject to RG 271.

clauses.section_name: B: Application of IDR requirements: Definition of 'complaint'
clauses.heading: Definition of 'complaint'
clauses.text: Firms must use the AS/NZS 10002:2014 definition: in summary, an expression of dissatisfaction made to or about an organisation, relating to its products, services, staff or complaint handling, where a response or resolution is explicitly or implicitly expected or legally required. Any expression of dissatisfaction meeting this definition must be handled through an IDR process that meets RG 271 (RG 271.28). 'About an organisation' is read to cover qualifying social media posts under RG 271.32(a).
subclauses: RG 271.28: expressions of dissatisfaction meeting the definition must go through the IDR process.
RG 271.29: for AFS licensees the IDR process must cover complaints against the licensee (s912A).

RG 271.30: firms must be proactive; a response is implicitly expected if the way the consumer raises the issue implies they expect action; the consumer does not need to use the word 'complaint' or put it in writing.
RG 271.31: firms should not label a complaint as feedback, an inquiry or a comment merely because it was verbal, the firm thinks it lacks merit, or a goodwill payment was made.
RG 271.33: not complaints include staff employment grievances, survey feedback or reports where no response is expected, and some hardship notices unless complaint issues are raised.
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraphs: RG 271.27 to RG 271.29. The single most important rule for conversational AI agents: the agent must detect complaints in ordinary conversation (including frustration about claim delays or decisions) without the customer using the word 'complaint', log them, and route them into IDR. Mislabelling complaints as feedback is a known failure mode (also flagged in ASIC REP 768). Not applicable to private health insurance health products.

clauses.section_name: B: Application of IDR requirements: Definition of 'complaint'
clauses.heading: Expressions of dissatisfaction that are complaints, including social media
clauses.text: The following are complaints: (a) posts meeting the complaint definition on a social media channel or account owned or controlled by the firm that is the subject of the post, where the author is identifiable and contactable; (b) objections to proposed superannuation death benefit distributions; (c) complaints about a matter in, or about, a remediation program; and (d) complaints about the handling of an insurance claim, such as excessive delays or unreasonable information requests.
subclauses: (a) Qualifying posts on the firm's own social media where the author is identifiable and contactable. Note 1: firms need not search third-party social media. Note 2: privacy must be protected when responding. Note 3: representatives must refer such complaints to their licensee.
(b) Objections to proposed superannuation death benefit distributions.
(c) Complaints about remediation programs or matters under remediation.
(d) Complaints about insurance claim handling, including delays or unreasonable information requests.
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraph (including notes). AI agents monitoring or responding on the insurer's own social channels must treat qualifying posts as complaints, move the conversation to a private channel to protect privacy, and start the IDR clock. Claim-handling dissatisfaction is expressly a complaint, which matters for claims chatbots.

clauses.section_name: C: IDR requirements: Acknowledgement of complaint
clauses.heading: Acknowledgement of complaint
clauses.text: Firms should acknowledge each complaint promptly. ASIC expects acknowledgement within 24 hours (or one business day) of receipt, or as soon as practicable. Acknowledgement may be verbal or written (email, post or social media), taking into account the channel the complainant used and any stated communication preferences (RG 271.52).
subclauses: RG 271.51: acknowledge within 24 hours or one business day, or as soon as practicable.
RG 271.52: acknowledgement may be verbal or written; consider the lodgement channel and the complainant's preferences.
clauses.notes: Not marked as an enforceable paragraph; it is an ASIC expectation, but it is the benchmark ASIC and AFCA use, and the General Insurance Code also sets acknowledgement standards. An AI agent can usually satisfy this in-channel immediately; it should tell the customer their complaint has been received and what happens next.

clauses.section_name: C: IDR requirements: What an IDR response must contain
clauses.heading: What an IDR response must contain
clauses.text: An IDR response is a written communication telling the complainant the final IDR outcome (either confirmation of actions taken to fully resolve the complaint, or the reasons for rejecting or partially rejecting it), their right to take the complaint to AFCA if dissatisfied, and AFCA's contact details. If the complaint is rejected in whole or part, the response must clearly give reasons by addressing the issues raised, stating findings on material facts with reference to supporting information, and giving enough detail for the complainant to decide whether to escalate (RG 271.54).
subclauses: (a) Final outcome at IDR, or reasons for rejection or partial rejection.
(b) Right to take the complaint to AFCA.
(c) AFCA contact details.
RG 271.54: reasons must address the issues, set out findings on material questions of fact with supporting information, and be detailed enough to support an informed escalation decision.
RG 271.55: detail should match complexity; no need to breach privacy or tipping-off laws.
RG 271.111 to RG 271.112: IDR responses and delay notifications must include AFCA access details.
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraphs: RG 271.53 to RG 271.54 (including notes). Any agent-generated final response must include the AFCA right and contact details and, where adverse, specific reasons tied to the evidence. Generic decline templates without findings of fact do not comply.

clauses.section_name: C: IDR requirements: Maximum timeframes for an IDR response
clauses.heading: When an IDR response must be provided by
clauses.text: A firm must give an IDR response no later than 30 calendar days after receiving the complaint, subject to different timeframes for some complaint types and to the delay exceptions. Time is calculated under s36 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901: the day of receipt is excluded, so day 1 is the first day after receipt, whether or not receipt was on a business day.
subclauses: Standard complaints (including insurance): no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.
Traditional trustee complaints: 45 calendar days (RG 271.76 to RG 271.78).
Superannuation trustee complaints other than death benefit distributions: 45 calendar days (RG 271.79), including insurance-in-super complaints lodged with the trustee.
Superannuation death benefit distribution complaints: 90 calendar days after expiry of the 28 calendar day objection period (RG 271.80 to RG 271.85).
Credit complaints involving default notices: 21 calendar days (RG 271.86, RG 271.91).
Credit complaints involving hardship notices or requests to postpone enforcement: 21 calendar days, with information-request and agreement variations (RG 271.92 to RG 271.93).

RG 271.64 to RG 271.66: a firm may exceed the maximum only if resolution is particularly complex or delayed by circumstances beyond its control, and it gives an IDR delay notification before the timeframe expires stating the reasons for the delay, the right to complain to AFCA, and AFCA's contact details.

RG 271.71: no IDR response needed if the complaint is closed by the end of the fifth business day after receipt because it was resolved to the complainant's satisfaction or an explanation or apology was given where no further action is reasonably possible.

RG 271.75: a written IDR response is still required within that 5 business day window if the complainant asks for one, or the complaint concerns hardship, a declined insurance claim, or the value of an insurance claim.
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraphs: RG 271.56 to RG 271.60 and Table 2; RG 271.64 to RG 271.66; RG 271.71; RG 271.75. For insurers the standard 30 calendar day clock applies (the General Insurance and Life Insurance Codes may set additional internal standards). A complaint logged by an AI agent starts the clock at receipt. Declined-claim and claim-value complaints always need a written IDR response with AFCA details, even if resolved quickly. Delay notifications must be sent before day 30.

clauses.section_name: C: IDR requirements: Maximum timeframes for an IDR response
clauses.heading: IDR delay notification
clauses.text: Before the relevant maximum timeframe expires, a firm that cannot respond in time because of complexity or circumstances beyond its control must give the complainant an IDR delay notification stating the reasons for the delay, their right to complain to AFCA if dissatisfied, and AFCA's contact details. The exceptions do not stop the complainant going to AFCA.
subclauses: (a) Reasons for the delay.
(b) Right to complain to AFCA.
(c) AFCA contact details.
RG 271.67 to RG 271.68: examples of complexity and of circumstances beyond the firm's control (for example waiting on third-party information or a required medical appointment).
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraph (RG 271.64 to RG 271.66 including notes). Workflow tooling should flag complaints approaching day 30 and generate compliant delay notifications.

clauses.heading: How to manage systemic issues
clauses.text: Boards must set clear accountabilities for complaints handling, including managing systemic issues identified through complaints (RG 271.118), and any reports to the board or executive committees must include complaint metrics and analysis, including systemic issues (RG 271.119). Firms must encourage and enable staff to escalate possible systemic issues from individual complaints, regularly analyse complaint data to identify systemic issues, promptly escalate possible systemic issues for investigation and action, and report internally on outcomes in a timely way. A systemic issue is one that affects, or could affect, more than one consumer (RG 271.117).
subclauses: (a) Encourage and enable staff to escalate possible systemic issues.
(b) Regularly analyse complaint data to identify systemic issues.
(c) Promptly escalate possible systemic issues for investigation and action.
(d) Report internally on investigation outcomes and actions in a timely manner.
RG 271.121: where a systemic issue is confirmed, ASIC expects prompt identification of affected consumers and fair remediation.
RG 271.123: AFCA must report systemic issues to the regulator within 15 calendar days after forming that view.
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraphs: RG 271.118 to RG 271.120 (including note). AI agents generate structured complaint data at scale; firms should use it for systemic issue detection, and an issue caused by the agent itself (for example a recurring wrong answer) is a systemic issue to escalate and, where relevant, assess for breach reporting under s912D.

clauses.section_name: E: IDR standards: Data collection, analysis and internal reporting
clauses.heading: Record all complaints
clauses.text: Firms must record all complaints received and have an effective system for recording complaint information that tracks the progress of each complaint. Firms should collect and analyse data such as volumes, nature, time to acknowledge and resolve, outcomes, systemic issues and AFCA escalations (RG 271.181 to RG 271.182), and must report complaints data regularly to senior management and the board (RG 271.183).
subclauses: RG 271.179: record every complaint and track its progress (enforceable).
RG 271.182: minimum data items to analyse.
RG 271.183: regular complaints reporting to senior management and the board (enforceable).
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraphs: RG 271.179 and RG 271.183. Every complaint detected by an AI agent must be written to the complaints system with timestamps; these records also feed ASIC IDR data reporting (Instrument 2022/205) and DDO complaints reporting to issuers (s994F(4)).

clauses.heading: Accessible IDR process
clauses.text: The IDR process must be easy to understand and use, including for people who need extra support. Firms should offer flexible lodgement channels, allow representatives to lodge on a consumer's behalf, and train staff to identify and assist people who need help (RG 271.135 to RG 271.139). The IDR process must be free to complainants (RG 271.141).
subclauses: RG 271.134: easy to understand and use.
RG 271.136 to RG 271.139: flexible channels, representatives, support for people needing assistance.
RG 271.141: IDR must be free.
clauses.notes: Enforceable paragraphs: RG 271.134 and RG 271.141 (also RG 271.142 to RG 271.143 on resourcing and staffing). An AI agent should not be the only complaint channel; customers must be able to reach a human and to complain about the agent itself.
